paragraphs.heading: A point on the surface
paragraphs.text: In seismology, the epicenter is the point on Earth's surface directly above the hypocenter, or focus. The focus is where an earthquake, or an explosion set off underground, originates. It is where the slipping of the fault begins. The rupture starts there and then spreads along the fault surface.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the first seismograms
paragraphs.text: The earliest seismographs were built to give a sense of the direction of an earthquake's first motions. A more precise location became possible once a time scale was added. Rather than just noting how far a pendulum moved, the instrument plotted its displacements on a moving graph driven by a clock mechanism. On these records the trace fell into two major portions. The P wave was the first seismic wave to arrive, and the S wave followed closely.

paragraphs.heading: From a time gap to a distance
paragraphs.text: The two kinds of wave travel at different velocities and take different paths through the Earth, and they arrive at different times. Geologists measure that time difference on a seismograph. They then find the distance on a travel-time graph at which the P wave and S wave are separated by the same amount. That gives the distance to the epicenter, which is called the epicentral distance.

paragraphs.heading: Why three stations
paragraphs.text: One seismograph gives a distance, but that can only be drawn as a circle, with an infinite number of possible places on it. Two seismographs give two circles that cross, which leaves two possible locations. Only a third seismograph gives a precise location. Locating an earthquake today still needs at least three seismometers. Once the distances from three or more stations are known, the point is found by a method called trilateration.

paragraphs.heading: Not always the worst-hit place
paragraphs.text: Before earthquakes were recorded by instruments, the epicenter was thought to be the place where the greatest damage occurred. Many people still hold the mistaken belief that the strongest shaking is always at the epicenter. In large earthquakes the greatest damage is often spread across the fault rupture zone instead. The direction of the rupture, an effect called directivity, can also put the area of greatest shaking away from the epicenter.

paragraphs.heading: The Denali earthquake
paragraphs.text: Alaska's Denali earthquake of 2002, at magnitude 7.9, is an example. Its epicenter was at the western end of the rupture. The greatest damage was about 330 km away, at the eastern end. Fault ruptures in large earthquakes can run for more than 100 km. When a fault ruptures from an epicenter at or near one end of the break, the waves along the fault are stronger in one direction.

paragraphs.heading: Earthquakes without instruments
paragraphs.text: For some earthquakes there is no instrumental data. The macroseismic epicenter is the best estimate of where the epicenter was, made without such data. It may be worked out from intensity data, from information about foreshocks and aftershocks, from knowledge of local fault systems, or by extrapolating from data on similar earthquakes. For historical earthquakes that were never recorded by instruments, a macroseismic epicenter is the only kind that can be given.
